name: Microsoft Word
tagline: The default word processor for business, school, and anyone who has ever been emailed a .docx.

pricing.basis: monthly per user, Word also sold in one-time Office Home bundles
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A text editor is a weekend project. Word is not a text editor, it is a file format that the entire working world treats as the unit of exchange, plus forty years of layout edge cases, plus the track changes and comments workflow that lawyers, editors, and academics actually run their jobs on. You can build something that opens and saves .docx, and it will work fine until the first document with nested tables, cross-references, footnotes, a style sheet, and a corporate template lands in your inbox and renders as soup. The thing you cannot build is everyone else having the same thing. If your documents never leave your laptop, write Markdown and be happier; if they do, the compatibility tax eats the project.
coreLoopDIY: A local rich text editor that imports and exports .docx reasonably well, keeps files on disk, and prints to PDF.
requirements: Node 20 and a modern Chromium browser for File System Access API
No accounts, no cloud, files stay in a local folder
whatYouLose: High fidelity .docx round-tripping: styles, numbering, footnotes, cross-references, nested tables, and corporate templates will degrade
Track changes, comments, and the whole review workflow people in legal and publishing refuse to work without
Real-time co-authoring, version history, and the SharePoint and OneDrive plumbing behind it
Native apps on Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android with offline sync and identical rendering
Pagination and print layout fidelity, mail merge, accessibility tooling, Copilot, and the grammar engine
moatNotes: The format is the lock-in. Every template, every court filing rule, every journal submission guideline assumes it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the document has to open correctly on someone else's machine, and that someone else is a client, a professor, a court clerk, or HR. Word is priced as part of a bundle most people already have for Excel and Outlook, so the marginal cost of the word processor feels like zero, which makes the compatibility risk of switching look irrational even when the alternative is genuinely nicer. Add the institutional layer: templates, macros, document management systems, and twenty years of files in a shared drive. Nobody is paying for the typing experience, they are paying for the interoperability guarantee.
notes: The editor is a weekend build; the format is not. The moat is .docx as the world's default interchange unit and every institution that requires it.
prompt:
Build a local-first rich text document editor called "Scribe" that opens and saves .docx files. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- TipTap (ProseMirror) for the editor
- mammoth for .docx import to HTML
- the docx npm package for .docx export
- Tailwind for styling
- No backend, no database, everything runs in the browser against local files

In scope:
- File System Access API: open a .docx or .md file from disk, edit, save back to the same handle with Ctrl+S
- A "Recent files" list persisted in IndexedDB holding file handles, with a permission re-request flow
- Formatting: bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, H1 to H3, bullet and ordered lists, blockquote, code block, horizontal rule, links, tables (insert, add or delete row and column), images embedded as base64
- A paragraph style dropdown mapped to a small fixed style set (Title, Heading 1 to 3, Body, Quote)
- Import: mammoth with a style map so Word headings and quotes land on the right TipTap nodes; show a dismissible banner listing anything dropped during import
- Export: serialize the TipTap doc to .docx via the docx package, covering every node type listed above; anything unsupported must throw a visible warning, never fail silently
- Also export to Markdown and to PDF via window.print with a print stylesheet sized for US Letter
- Word count, character count, and reading time in a status bar
- Autosave to IndexedDB every 5 seconds as crash insurance, separate from explicit file saves
- Keyboard shortcuts for all formatting, a distraction-free mode, and dark mode

Out of scope, do not attempt and do not stub:
- Track changes, comments, real-time collaboration, mail merge, macros
- Pixel-accurate pagination or matching Word's line breaking
- Any cloud sync or login

Deliverables: working app on npm run dev, a README that states plainly which .docx features survive round-tripping and which do not, and a test fixture folder with three sample .docx files (simple, tables, messy corporate template) plus notes on how each one imports.
